text: Everybody can take their seats. Well, first off, good morning, everyone. I want to thank everybody for being here, and at least for me, and I think for many of us, kind of, we had a very, very busy weekend, and it was one, I think, quite enjoyable, I think, would be the way that I would start it.

And maybe the best part of the weekend was the Mount Vernon Town meeting, right? You all were there? We had a great time, and I appreciate the chairman and county executive being there and our school board member, and then many, many, many, many, many, many more county staff and not-for-profits, et cetera, were there just to, frankly, connect and share the community with each of us.

The other thing I wanted to mention was we had really a wonderful time receiving the venerable monks who had walked all the way from Texas just to see us. No, I'm sorry, they didn't. They were walking for peace, and that really had a nerve, and I don't know if the chairman wants to make any comments about that.

Yeah, I would be glad to. It was wonderful. I think probably what was most wonderful to me is to see the thousands of people in Fairfax County who came out both along the walking route and then also at the Buddhist temple where we had an opportunity to have lunch with them to come out and see them.

And I think, you know, as I said earlier today on the news, my kind of takeaway from the entire event was when they shared with us that, you know, take a moment each day to write down, this is my peaceful day on a sheet of paper before you venture out to do the other things you're going to do during the day, just as a calm, peaceful reminder to all of us that, you know, peace starts with ourselves, peace starts at home, and it was just great to see them all turn out.

And secondly, and I know you want to add to this, Supervisor Stork, I do want to particularly thank Major Morrow, our Mount Vernon District Police Department, and Chief Butler, who took the time to come out also and greet them and give them a token of appreciation from our public safety agencies.

But, you know, to put on an event like that, a major undertaking, to handle intersections along Richmond Highway on a busy weekend is a major undertaking. and the way in which our first responders protected the public, protected them, but still allowed the public to come out and share in the moment was exceptional.

So all around a great day. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Well said. And I also want to thank the public because we're closing down Route 1 and other major roads is never easy, and I'm sure frustrated a number of individuals. But I hope they all recognize those short-term impacts, hopefully create a larger sense of what we need and how important it is for us all to work together, be together, and frankly, walk for peace and be peaceful and find our peace.

We have a number of things going on this morning. I'm going to get to it. First and foremost, we had a meeting a few months ago. Did anybody have any comments or questions or changes in the notes that were sent out to everyone. If not, we will get right to it. Good morning. Our first topic for today is a board matter, frankly, from Chairman McKay on Fairfax County's economic competitiveness. It was introduced last August. Staff will provide an current economic trends, an overview of the county's competitive position, and this will include how the federal workforce

changes are really affecting all of us, the sector growth patterns and emerging opportunities. And we know the core of that is emergency opportunities. And I know others will maybe mention this, but we have a significant SpaceX conference next week and look forward to all being part of that that can join us. Our economy and business opportunities continue to demonstrate remarkable resilience. I know we have all fearful a year ago what that impact would be. There's impact, clearly. Our unemployment rate's gone up. Some of the challenges in continuing the energy

that we had before, it's been kind of pushed back a little bit. But I know that we have a very strong economy, very strong, and very incredibly resourceful and smart and capable workforce here. And so we know that we're going to be able to capitalize on the opportunities that are always there, frankly, as well as proactively address the challenges that are emerging.

So the economic data that you'll see today represents an important first step, first step in the team's ongoing analysis. This information, combined with our continued monitoring and stakeholder engagement, will directly inform the strategic recommendations currently in development.

In addition to economic trends, the team will briefly highlight our recent business and workforce assistance initiatives. This serves as both a reminder of the resources available to our constituents as well as a demonstration of the tangible impact these programs are having, impacts we can build upon going forward.

While we don't have a formal presentation, the meeting materials include an analysis of small business pandemic relief programs. If we have time at the end, Rebecca Bodry will provide a brief summary of the positive impacts of these programs. The second topic today, we'll propose an expanded and updated revitalization and redevelopment economic incentive program, something that's important really to all of our county, but particularly those revitalization areas.

This is really an important tool in our arsenal to spur local economic development. During the presentations, discussions today, please keep partnership opportunities in mind. I think that's probably the most important thing is partnership opportunities. We know it's a collaborative process.

We know we have to engage and build upon different strengths that the business community has or education or other communities have, as well as what the county can do to support that. Particularly with the Commonwealth, we know we'll be hopefully engaging with them and having maybe a future meeting.

We'll be having the Commonwealth representatives here, as well as the Fairfax County success in Virginia, which spurs, frankly, Virginia's success. As you review this data, consider how these challenges and opportunities might be addressed through our advocacy efforts in Richmond. I'll now turn it over to the Deputy County Executive, Jen Miller, for some brief remarks to introduce our first topic and then moving to Stephen Tordidi with the Mechanic Development Authority.

So thank you both. Thank you all. Thank you, Supervisor Stork. I'm Jennifer Miller, the Deputy County Executive for Community Development, and I wanted to put this in a little bit of context, and Supervisor Stork has done that, but also to lay out and tie together a timeline that we'll be talking about.

So as mentioned, this was one of two big board matters rolled out, this one on August 26th, and that as a result of this a couple weeks later in early September, there was also a board matter related to housing. They ended up with a little bit of overlap and blended and tied nicely together.

So this is the completion of the first step of the economic board matter. The other matters include two that overlap with the housing board matter, which we'll be talking about a little bit this afternoon, specifically the how do we add housing inventory and affordability, and then also how we look at the development process.

So as part of the housing board matter, we're looking at the development process specific to housing. But as part of this matter, we're looking at economic development writ large. We did share a timeline, but for those who don't have it in front of them, just to quickly address where we are. The committee has been meeting, the task force has been meeting for a while.

as I mentioned, this is the first step of completion of that process. By the end of this month, we will have all of the initiative completed. We then plan to roll that out to the development community on March 19th in a meeting that we'll be having that will address both the housing and the economic competitiveness matter to get input from the development community on whether those things we're doing as part of this task force seem effective, which ones they believe will be most effective. We'll then implement that into a plan that we'll be sharing with the board in late April and briefing in its full completion on May 12th, along with the housing

board matter. So again, these board matters tie together nicely, but the important part here is laying the foundation. We all know that there are some challenges, even though we've had successes that we can address in Fairfax County with our economic competitiveness. And the intent for this is to lay out the facts and data that served as the baseline for what we'll be rolling into the Initiatives that we'll be completing at the end of this month. So with that, thanks to our partners at EDA Thank you very much Jen for the introduction and thank you as well as supervisor stork for the introduction and

Appreciate the board giving me this opportunity to speak on a very important topic as Jen was just mentioning this is The purpose of today's presentation is to give us a baseline understanding or a common understanding of currently where we stand their local economy using various economic indicators and trends and this is extremely important at this moment because 2025 was very much a dynamic year we saw multiple changes and shifts you know across various indicators which I'll get into in a second so we're going to be taking a look at the workforce and

the business and industry indicators in the office market indicators which you'll see is a bit of a mixed bag but first starting with workforce, which is very much top of mind. Due to federal government impacts, we're thinking about reductions in force and the deferred resignation program. You can see that Fairfax County resident population was certainly not immune to those impacts. And we did see over

a 1% jump in unemployment year over year. We can make this assumption on those impacts based upon the similar trends that we see both at the county level and the D.C. region level. So I also thought it was important to include the Commonwealth of Virginia and the U.S.

to see how those changes compare. We did see, we got fresh data for December this past Friday. We did see a slight decrease in the unemployment rate, but there's also some seasonality to that if we think about the holiday season and ramping up of hiring.

But hopefully this is a trend that we see continue, you know, a reversal of the trend from the previous year. Like I said, when we're trying to understand really where these impacts are coming from, you know, right now we're relying on regional data and place of work data versus resident and population information.

But you can see in this year over year change, both for the D.C. region and northern Virginia, Similar decrease in the federal employment, so a 14% reduction. Also a note that this does not include the national security workforce in there in the way that the state is collected, which may dampen the percentage reduction.

But we did feel a disproportionate impact compared to the U.S., which saw a 10% reduction in federal government employees. You can see some of the largest agencies that took those reductions. And even though, you know, these previous two data points are changes, certainly a call to action, and we have been responsive in that way.

It's important to keep these changes in unemployment and provide some context around them. So historically, Fairfax County has a very tight labor market. Our unemployment rate is traditionally in any normal economic cycle below 3%.

But when we look at peer jurisdictions, either those that have similar industry characteristics or demographic characteristics, even with the changes that we've seen in the past year, kind of puts us right in the middle of the pack here. So really one way to look at the data, and I know it's easier to look at sort of this D.C. region bubble, but also compare it to the rest of the nation, some of those counties that we compete for projects with.

Another way to look at the changes in employment is in a historical context. If the dust has settled on this employment reduction, this event is very similar to both the dot-com bubble and the great financial crisis, those employment reductions.

So we want to take a look at how long did those past events take to recover? Why did the employment boost back up? And if there's any insights that we can take away from that. For instance, the dot-com bubble, that was a three-year timeline to recover our previous workforce levels.

That was due to a compounding of not only the tech employment that was lost by the bubble burst, But then adding on to that, post 9-11, we saw a dip in employment in the D.C. region for leisure and hospitality. One thing that did happen that helped accelerate or reignite growth in employment, one component, was tech hiring.

Those members of the workforce who lost their jobs in the dot-com bouleverse, the more established tech firms came in and brought that employment back up. Different story for the great financial crisis. It was a two-year timeline to recover our workforce. We didn't see nearly the same jumps of unemployment rates as we did across the country.

We were more insulated. This was probably because of the federal government's intervention to provide support and resources during this recession. Another way we can look at the information is to go down to the industry level. And before you have the information on our professional services industry, This is our largest industry in Fairfax County.

It makes up about a quarter of our employment base, encompasses many of the government contractors and much of our tech workforce. It's a very dense and rich talent pool that we've had here, as you can see evidenced by the concentration. We have the largest concentration of this employment base in the U.S., three times the U.S. average.

The next county in the terms of concentration is San Francisco County at about two and a half. So it really speaks volumes to, again, the talent pool that we have existing here. What we're seeing, though, is a bit of a plateauing of the growth rate and even a little bit of a negative dip in the past five years of this employment.

So what we're taking a look at is how could we reignite that growth? How are we going to dissect this industry? One way that we can look at this is in artificial intelligence professional services. So the latest CBRE Tech Talent Report had the DC region as the number one talent pool for AI professional business services talent.

That's something that maybe we can use and dig deeper on and find if there's opportunities to accelerate that growth. Another action we can take is to look at, and that we are taking, is looking at some of our recent growth industries and how we can either foster that environment or help accelerate the growth of those industries.

The top one, computing infrastructure, the first thought that might come across people's heads is data centers. And while certainly supporting that industry, and that does fall within this, much of the growth that we've seen here in the county is more of the office using employment. If you think about a major employer like Amazon Web Services, they've been growing their employment base here, and they fall within that industry category.

Another one is Enabled Intelligence, a smaller company. But they fall under this industry code. And they've been growing as well, providing data processing services as an AI company. And then if we're thinking about what we have here, the digital infrastructure, how do we leverage that to possibly capture demand in emerging technologies?

We think about quantum computing. We have a lot of foundational assets that could play well into that future growth. So are there any other emerging industries that really would complement the existing and growing digital infrastructure. Scientific research and development is a really intriguing one that we've been seeing growing.

If we're thinking about the federal government, the administration's priorities, they're looking for a lot of the, you know, build me the product, let me see it, the prototyping. We could see growth accelerate there, but having the physical space or physical infrastructure to allow those technologies to grow or to be prototyped is going to be very pivotal going forward.

And that also introduces the topic of dual-use technologies. We're seeing a rise here in the county of, if you think about drones, cybersecurity services, AI, not only developing products for the federal government, but being able to pivot to the civilian sector.

And then satellite telecommunications. Supervisor Stork talked about the Space Next Conference. It's going to be a great opportunity to use a growing industry in our county and leverage that for future growth in the new space economy. Latest figures show that the global space economy is about $630 billion, and by 2035, that could go up to $1.8 trillion.

So there's a lot of runway to work with, and we have a lot of the foundational assets. Again, how do we, you know, rev the engine and accelerate that growth in that sector? And then management of companies or headquarters. This is an industry that we see continued, sustained growth in, but that relies on a stable, pro-business-friendly environment, access to talent, quality of life measures, and infrastructure, which we all have here.

So, you know, that's something that we're going to look to continue and see if there's ways that we could also accelerate that. And I was talking about that access to talent, and we're going to need the workforce, and that comes from the population. So we thought this is very much something worth monitoring.

If we're thinking about the early years in COVID, we saw an increase in domestic out-migration here in Fairfax County and a slowdown of international migration. Those trends have kind of reversed in the last few years where domestic out-migration has continued to dwindle, where international migration has spiked up and, again, providing us with more of that talent pool.

The big question going forward is going to be what happens with the international migration. The U.S., for the first time in 50 years, saw a negative net international migration. So how does that apply to the local level? It's information that we're really interested in seeing and dissecting.

Looking at other indicators, GDP, this reflects the size and the growth of your economy. And we have this at the local level. I will note that this measure includes Fairfax City and the City of Falls Church. But again, two of the main takeaways from here is if you look at the two periods, the great financial crisis and COVID-19, those were the two most recent periods where we did see negative growth, pointing to that next year's growth and really rebounding.

And that speaks upon the resilience that our economy has here and how quick we're able to rebound. Also, just the general size and share of our economy. If you look at the Commonwealth of Virginia or the D.C. metro region, we make up a quarter of both of those economies, which really speaks volumes to what we have here and what we need to continue to grow.

Federal procurement, while we're in the midst of diversifying our economy for sure, We want to make sure we're keeping tabs on this. We were moderately surprised to see that we saw a year-over-year increase in federal procurement dollars to Fairfax County-based companies.

This is by place of performance, and especially given the narrative that was coming in the first half of 2025, we weren't sure where the numbers were going to head. And while we do have a dense concentration of defense contracts, we also do have a very large portion of civilian contracts. So my main takeaway here is when you think about the Fairfax County-based government contractors here, for the most part, although we did see layoff events, they were able to sustain employment levels, and that also translates into keeping occupied office

or an industrial and commercial space. We're also seeing the convergence of the venture capital community with federal procurement, and we're seeing elevated levels of dollars coming into Fairfax-based companies. While we're still finalizing the Q4 numbers, it's looking like we're going to cross the $1 billion mark for the fifth year in a row. This is very important because there's this growing narrative around a lot of venture capital shops setting up shop in the D.C. region. One very interesting one, Andreasen Horowitz, one of the top global VC

firms open a D.C. office. And then more recently, Booz Allen Hamilton announced a partnership with that VC firm where they're going to have access to their portfolio and they're going to help them with speed to market and have an understanding of how the federal government process works. But they also noted they're also going to, you know, the non-government contractor companies or those not looking for that, they're also going to assist there. So there's some demand to capture there, and we're interested to see if these levels will continue to increase going forward.

But, you know, when we're still looking at our market compared to other markets, we're still very much a small piece of the pie, but we do believe there is a lot of that pie to go after, and there's going to be growing interest in that going forward. We, you know, we're looking at new business starts in the county, and while those levels are elevated when we look at some of our peer competitors, we're not really adding the same level of new businesses. So when we're thinking about the startup ecosystem, again, a lot of room to grow with the dollars that are coming in. We just want to be able to create that flywheel to

have new companies start here. And then from a consumer sentiment perspective, we like to look at taxable sales at the local level to see how the changes from the federal government and our workforce may have impacted spending. We're still waiting on Q4 numbers, but so far it looks like the levels really have not been impacted, which is good news to see there in the county and on the regional level. And then we recorded some welcome news in the office market. So after

five consecutive years of vacancy rate increases, we recorded the first year-over-year decrease in office market vacancy rate going down to 17.4%. A couple of the contributing factors to this was the continued removal of obsolete high vacancy office product and replacing that with new higher tax replacement inventory. In fact, we had over a million square feet of office inventory taken offline in this past year and either plan for redevelopment, so

demolition of that product or adaptive reuse. We're also seeing the end of our speculative office construction pipeline. So those office projects that don't have a committed tenant, which if they do deliver vacant, that could bump up the vacancy rate. But it's good news that the trophy office market is performing well here in the county. And then more of our employers are determining their office footprint. So we're really getting to an understanding of where our workforce resides, how often they're coming into the office, and what future office space needs will be long term.

So while there still are companies that are contracting their footprint, the rate of that is starting to decline, while we're starting to see an increase in those companies who are adding their footprint. They're realizing, okay, well, maybe, yeah, based upon how many people I might have coming in on a Wednesday, even if it's Wednesday, I need to accommodate all of them.
So certainly welcome news in that regard, but if we're thinking about a call to action for the office market, it still very much is a bifurcated office market here in the county.

So the top product is seeing very healthy demand, and the vacancy rate continues to go down, while some of our Class B, C product continues to lose tenants and is seeing the vacancy rate growing up. So if a landlord is not deciding to put capital into a major renovation of an older product and cannot capture that new demand, then we need to figure out what is the next steps for that inventory.

And we have about 7 million square feet of office product that is slated for demolition. From the business attraction side, this is really important for us to have a site selector community that we're constantly trying to receive feedback from.

The site selectors are representing these office and industrial projects where they're trying to decide where to relocate or where to expand to. So they really care about the depth of local knowledge that the community has and also their competitors as well.

They want to know that there's speed to market. And by that, I mean being very responsive, but also being very transparent about your operating environment, as well as the office building or the site that you're proposing. And then this same community, there's several groups that put out yearly rankings of priorities.

And so this is being fed from those companies that are making these decisions. And while talent is still up there in priorities, infrastructure is really coming in as a top priority, which bodes well for our community, given the investments that we put both in the digital infrastructure and the physical infrastructure.

So all in all, we certainly took a hit to our workforce. We're not naive to that fact. But we see some early green shoots as far as the dollars that are coming in and the companies and the industries that are growing here.

So it really comes down to that opportunity of now is the moment where those dollars are being fed in for poised growth of those companies. How are we creating that environment going forward where that company knows, hey, when I grow, I'm going to grow here and have the access to talent?

So that's something that we want to dissect. We're making sure we're taking a look at all of our competitors in that regard and doing a lot of self-evaluation in that sense. So, again, a bit of a mixed bag, but, you know, I know we're going to be, you know, using this data and the deeper dive of each pieces of this information as part of our recommendations.

And we know that we need to have, and Supervisor Stark, I'll close with this, you were talking about strategic partnerships are going to be very vital going forward. So I'll stop there and I'll, you know, see if there's any questions or comments. And thanks again. Steve, well, thank you very much. And just maybe at a high level, any particular surprises as you went and put this stuff together? Any particular things that, oh, I didn't really expect that that would be what I would see when bringing all this data together?

Yes, that's a great question, Supervisor. The growth of the computing infrastructure employment, when I was diving more into that, seeing that it's, you know, again, I brought it up, the first thought is, okay, well, we're thinking about the data centers, but the data processing, the combination of AI and data processing, and the support of digital infrastructure is more so growing our office sector. There's companies that they may be supporting the data center community, but they're taking office space in Fairfax County, which is promising to see. So

that was a little bit of an aha moment. And, you know, there's plenty more of those. You know, wasn't very surprised by the growth in the satellite telecommunications industry, but it's more so is motivating to see, okay, you know, how do we capture lightning in a bottle and make sure that we're promoting and accelerating that growth. Thank you. Mr. Chairman. Yeah, just, and I think I know the answer to this, but because we live in the DMV area, there's always concern over the data in terms of actually reflecting what's happening in the county, since we know that some of the jobs lost are not filled by people who are in the county. And we

also know that some of the private sector jobs that are lost are filled by people outside of Fairfax County. They're not necessarily filled by Fairfax County residents. And so was there anything in your data that led you to believe how we are kind of stacking up against others in the DMV area? And when we look at these job numbers, do you think it's a wash? In other words, like when you look at the number of positions that have been lost, do you think it's pretty evenly spread throughout the DMV area? Or do you feel like there's a disproportionate impact on Fairfax County? And if so, how would we know that? That's a great question, Chairman. And we really rely on

the resident population unemployment statistics. What's a little bit frustrating right now is we don't know how that cross cuts, so we can't really see the characteristics of those employed at this moment for the latest data. When we do look at unemployment rates compared to other neighboring jurisdictions in the region, we do think that, you know, we weren't as hard hit as some of those other resident populations. So that's what we can use right now until we get more of the industry-based information.

But that's also why we rely on some of the federal procurement data, you know, the dollars coming in, because that can signal that, again, that, you know, maybe that wasn't as hard hit or, in fact, grew in Fairfax County, where in the rest of the D.C. region, we saw that number go down and, you know, may be able to attribute that to our defense community.

And something I didn't mention before, but defense tech is a buzzword that keeps coming up. Northern Virginia is the number one region in the U.S. for defense tech contracts, which is just going to continue to be a priority going forward. Yeah, and I think that kind of goes to my second point, which is, you know, in identifying our niche areas, you know, is there clarity in what those are? And it sounds like there is some clarity on that. And then what next steps do we need to do or what are we missing to make sure we execute this moment? Because everyone in the region is going to be challenged to try to, you know, retrieve and recoup some of these jobs. We

want to obviously be doing that better than anyone else. I mean, we operate as one region, we're regional partners, but at the end of the day, our first interest is in making sure that the county, our workforce, and that our businesses respond most favorably. And so as we move forward, understanding and continuing to double down on those niche areas will help us fully recover from this depression, for lack of a better descriptor, quicker than anyone else in the region, and we need to be constantly mindful of that.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I'm going to come up the road, and I'm going to start with Supervisor Lusk. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Really appreciate the presentations. Good to see you again, Stephen. Could I ask on the venture capital slide, so this is great.

We've gotten past a billion and projected to do that again. I'm recalling the first time we did it was in 2000, $1.25 billion. So the question I have on this slide is, when we look at the disbursement of investment, how much of it is going to earlier stage opportunities versus later stage opportunities?

Yeah, that's a great question. And thank you for that, Supervisor Lusk. Yeah, we have a breakdown on that. I will note that the larger rounding funds are making up a good portion of the funding that we're seeing.

If we think about a company like ID.me, they received a large rounding fund. So I think that's a great note to emphasize is that when we're talking about those new business starts, that startup ecosystem, dollars are coming in where there's a lot more of that pyre, that runway that we can capture, especially for the early seed companies.

I will note, and Supervisor Sork, I'm sorry, I didn't mention this before, but when we're looking at the companies that are receiving funding, we actually saw an uptick in both clean tech and health tech companies, very young companies that are seeing funding rounds and are headquartered here in the county.

So that's promising from an industry diversification. Yeah, I mean, I think the important thing is that we've got to have the ability to support those emerging earlier stage companies because those are the ones that are going to be the bigger companies later on. You've got to have a pipeline for that.

And then the second question I wanted to ask is on the pipeline. So thinking about where we were, and this may be more for Anna, where we were in terms of prospects a year ago versus where we are today in terms of prospects as it relates to square footage requests.

So trying to get a sense of are we tracking in a place that is stronger than last year or is it more similar to last year? So what I would say is last year we were looking at a huge contraction, as you were aware. Yep. This year we have been looking at a modest growth in new investment coming into the county, but we're definitely tracking most of them under 50,000 square feet. We have some mega projects, though, that are surfacing across the country now, and it's definitely a sign of

deliberate decision-making at the point of where we're kind of seeing two competing realities being true at the same time. You have this uncertainty up here, which we all experience and we've been experience in the county, but we have incredible investment coming from federal government and private sector at the same time. And a lot of that is actually international. So the decisions are taking longer, which you know in the past they have been a lot faster. So we're seeing a movement to the growth side. And on the pipeline, we're still seeing these midsize movements, but we're

starting to see signals for the larger deals coming to play. The competition is really, really stiff though as you can imagine what i would say though is for the capital piece of this what we probably don't most often communicate as a as a collective is yes we have the vc funding capital over here but if you if you look at the chart where you saw san francisco outpacing everyone you put the federal government contract funding on top of our you know capital attraction we beat out every region in this country. So considering the fact that federal government right now is really

focusing on pushing that investment to the private sector, we're seeing some of our non-profit and research partners coming to the table to talk about how do we cultivate the startups ecosystem with not just that capital funding, but including federal. So there's a huge opportunity there.

That's great. And then last is on the question of incentives. So acknowledging that we have had support from the state over a period of time and that we've had less support, just trying to understand where are we as it relates to support from the state for incentive packages.

What I would say right now, most of the deals that have incentives attached to them, we bring to the state to solicit their support, and we're not seeing any pushback on them supporting us. They're at the table helping, and this is at the ground level, obviously. However, I know this task force that Jen Miller and Rebecca are spearheading for economic competitiveness from the board matter is looking at how do we evolve?

Because the way that we have incented these projects, as you're aware in the past, may not be as effective moving into the future as we're seeing more deals coming in that require those incentives. But the state right now is at the table on multiple deals we're working on.

And I'm very positive on that. That's great. Thank you very much. Thank you, Supervisor Palachuk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you so much, Steve and Anna and the team. Actually, my question falls on a little bit of the last one around incentives, which I will call kind of the big elephant in the room here.

But I'm wondering a little bit, right, at the local level. I was just reading this morning about Maryland quantum computing and the state support there and how even with that they then lost one of the largest businesses, right, with their investment with support from the governor. So I guess, you know, what we control here. So first of all, it's kind of a two-part question.
